concept.name: Yield to maturity
concept.definition: The annual rate of return an investor earns if a bond is bought at its current price and held to maturity, with all coupons reinvested at that same rate; equivalently, the single discount rate that equates the present value of the bond's remaining cash flows to its current price.
concept.intuition: YTM is the bond's all-in interest rate: it folds the coupon stream and the gain or loss to par into one annualized number, letting different bonds be compared on equal footing.
concept.mechanics: YTM is found by solving P = sum_t C_t/(1+y)^t + F/(1+y)^T for y given the price — in general only by trial and error or numerical solver. Price and YTM move inversely: when market rates rise, the price of a fixed-rate bond falls and its YTM rises. For semiannual-pay bonds, the periodic rate found is conventionally doubled to quote YTM (bond-equivalent basis).
concept.formula: P = sum_{t=1..T} C/(1+y)^t + F/(1+y)^T, where P = current price, C = periodic coupon, F = face value, T = number of periods, y = yield to maturity per period (solved numerically).
concept.failure_modes: YTM overstates realized return when coupons cannot be reinvested at the same rate, and it is irrelevant for bonds not held to maturity; for callable bonds, YTM assumes a maturity that may never occur (yield-to-worst or yield-to-call is more appropriate).
concept.misconceptions: YTM is not the coupon rate and not a guaranteed return: it holds only under reinvestment at the YTM and no default, and it says nothing about price risk if the bond is sold early.
concept.example: A 6-year bond with an 8% coupon and $1,000 face quoted at $955.14 has a yield to maturity of about 9%, found by solving the price equation by trial and error.
